title: Snāna Yātrā
body:
The Snāna Yātrā, also known as the Deva Snāna Pūrṇimā, is one of the most vibrant and magnificent festivals of the Jagannātha tradition. Celebrated on the full-moon day of the month of Jyeshtha, it is the ceremonial bathing, the abhishekam, of Lord Jagannātha, together with Lord Balabhadra and Devī Subhadrā.

On this day the deities are brought out of the sanctum of the twelfth-century Sri Jagannātha Temple at Puri and placed on the Snāna Maṇḍapa, a platform built for this sacred event. It is a rare occasion on which devotees from every walk of life, including those who may not enter the temple, can see the Lord in His full glory. As the Vedic mantras resound and the conches blow, one hundred and eight pots of sanctified water drawn from the Sunā Kuā, the golden well, are poured over the deities. The ritual is a symbol of divine cleansing, and it also reveals the Lord's boundless compassion: He allows Himself to be touched by the elements and seen by all.

The Skanda Purāṇa, the Padma Purāṇa and the Jagannātha Māhātmya give this event its theological setting. According to these texts, the Snāna Yātrā re-enacts the bathing ceremonies offered to Lord Vishnu in His various incarnations, as Vāmana, Varāha or Rāma. Though Lord Jagannātha's form is of wood, the dāru mūrti, His presence is fully divine, and His bath is no mere outward ritual but an act of cosmic love, purification and mercy.

The day begins with the Pahandi, a grand procession in which the deities are carried from the inner sanctum to the Snāna Maṇḍapa. The first to come out is Sudarshana, followed by Lord Balabhadra, Devī Subhadrā and finally Lord Jagannātha. In the afternoon the Gajapati Mahārāja, the titular king of Puri and the foremost of the Lord's servitors, sweeps the bathing platform in the ritual called the Chhera Pahanra, a sign of humility before the Lord. The deities are then dressed in the Gaja Vesha, an adornment that shows them in the form of the elephant-headed Gaṇesha, signifying that their divinity embraces all.

After the bath the deities retire to a secluded chamber, the Anavasara Ghar, where they remain out of public view for fourteen days. This period is the Anavasara Līlā, in which the Lord seems to fall ill from the cold of His bath. The temple's traditional physician, the Baidya, gives Him herbal medicines, and the devotees know the mood of vipralambha bhakti, the sweet pain of separation from the Lord. The līlā shows that even in separation love deepens and longing grows.

The devotees then wait eagerly for the Netrotsava, the festival of the eyes, held just before the Ratha Yātrā, when they receive their first glimpse of the deities renewed in fresh, youthful forms, the Nabajaubana Darshan, just before the Lord and His brother and sister mount their great chariots for the procession.

The Snāna Yātrā is more than a ritual: it embodies the Lord's accessibility. Lord Jagannātha, whose very name means the Lord of the Universe, steps out of His sanctum for everyone, and so affirms the heart of bhakti, that God is not confined by boundaries, hierarchy or caste. Seeing the Lord bathed, adorned and lovingly cared for, we are reminded that the divine is both majestic and intimate, grand yet near, transcendent yet immanent.
